segments.text: Almost every solid sinks in its own liquid. Drop solid wax into melted wax, and it sinks. So why does ice float on water?
Here is the surprise. Liquid water at four degrees Celsius is denser than ice, about one gram per cubic centimeter versus point nine two.
The reason lives inside the molecule. Each water molecule has one oxygen and two hydrogens, bent at about one hundred and four degrees.
Oxygen pulls electrons toward itself, so it is slightly negative and the hydrogens slightly positive. Neighboring molecules attract through hydrogen bonds.
In liquid water, molecules tumble around. Bonds constantly break and reform, so molecules can crowd close together.
When water freezes, molecules lock into a hexagonal lattice. Each one bonds to four neighbors at fixed angles, which holds them farther apart.
The lattice is full of empty space. Packed this way, the same molecules take up about nine percent more volume, so ice is lighter per unit volume.
Lighter per volume means it floats, with about nine tenths of an iceberg below the surface. Notice the ice sits mostly submerged.
So ice floats because hydrogen bonds force water into an open lattice when it freezes. That floating layer insulates lakes, letting life survive winter below.
